name: IXL (IXL Learning)
origin_region: Global, US-origin (IXL Learning, San Mateo, California). Operates localized country sites for the US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India, Singapore and South Africa. Expanded internationally by acquisition - Rosetta Stone, Wyzant, Teachers Pay Teachers, and in May 2025 the UK live-tutoring company MyTutor, its first internationally based acquisition.
target_age: Pre-K through grade 12 (math runs Pre-K to Calculus). The SD/primary-relevant band is Pre-K to grade 6.
delivery_mode: online-app (browser plus iOS/Android apps), sold both to schools and directly to families. Since the 2025 MyTutor acquisition IXL is drifting toward hybrid: live human 1-to-1 tutoring by university-student tutors is now part of the group, but that is a separate UK-centric service, not a feature inside the IXL practice product.
language_localization: No Bahasa Indonesia. Child UI, question text, explanations and parent reports are English. Spanish exists as a subject to learn and there is some Spanish-language support, but not Indonesian. An Indonesian SD child would have to read every math word problem in English - which, given that reading errors are one of the error types we care about, actively confounds diagnosis for this market. [uncertain] the exact extent of IXL's Spanish interface localization.
pricing_model: subscription. US family membership (as posted in 2026): approximately $9.95/month or $79/year for one subject; approximately $15.95/month or $129/year for math plus language arts; approximately $19.95/month or $159/year for the core-subjects package (Math Pre-K to Calculus, Language Arts Pre-K-12, Science K to Physics, Social Studies K-12). Each additional child adds roughly $4/month or $40/year. School/district site licences are priced separately. There is no meaningful free tier - unpaid users get only a small number of questions per day. At roughly IDR 150,000-320,000 per month this is priced for US households, not for the mainstream Indonesian SD parent. [uncertain] exact current figures; pricing pages resisted automated fetch and numbers come from aggregator/review sources.
local_curriculum_alignment: No Kurikulum Merdeka or K13 alignment. IXL aligns to US state standards and Common Core, and for its country sites to the English National Curriculum, Ontario, the Australian Curriculum, Indian boards and Singapore syllabi. Indonesia is not a supported curriculum region, so skill sequencing, notation conventions and assessment framing do not map to what an Indonesian SD teacher or an OSN-track parent expects. [uncertain] whether any partner-led Indonesian standards mapping exists.
does_error_type_diagnosis: no (at best partial, and not in the sense that matters). This confirms and sharpens the earlier finding. IXL has two things that look like diagnosis and are not: (1) Trouble Spots, which is a QUANTITY TRIGGER - a trouble spot fires when a student misses three questions within a specific item type inside a skill. It tells you WHICH item type the child keeps missing and lets an adult scroll the actual missed questions, but it never says WHY: no label distinguishing a misread question from a conceptual misconception from an arithmetic slip. The adult must read the missed questions and infer the cause themselves. (2) The Real-Time Diagnostic, which is a LEVEL ESTIMATOR - it re-calibrates difficulty and reports a working grade level per strand. It is psychometric placement, not error analysis. Nothing in IXL's official diagnostic documentation, its FAQ blog post, or its teacher guides mentions misconceptions or error types at all.
diagnosis_granularity: A combination of topic-mastery-map and trouble-spot-quantity - explicitly NOT mcq-distractor-mapped-misconception and not a full error-type taxonomy. Concretely: (a) SmartScore per skill, 0-100, mastery-style, which rises and falls with correctness, question difficulty, recency and consistency; (b) diagnostic levels on a 0-800+ scale where the number encodes working grade level - a level of 400 means readiness to start 4th-grade skills and 450 means about halfway through the 4th-grade curriculum, with preschool at 0-50 and kindergarten at 50-100; levels are reported per strand via the Diagnostic Strand Analysis; (c) Trouble Spots at item-type granularity, triggered at three misses. The finest resolution IXL ever reaches is 'this child keeps missing this item type' - one step short of 'this child believes something false, and here is what'.
diagnosis_input_modality: mcq-distractor plus short typed/numeric free response and interactive manipulatives (drag-and-drop, number lines, graph plotting). There is NO capture of the child's written working: no free-response OCR of a photographed worksheet, no handwriting-stroke capture, no video-explained reasoning, no self-report of strategy. This is the structural reason IXL cannot classify error type even if it wanted to - it only ever sees the final answer, so a right answer reached by guessing and a right answer reached by understanding are indistinguishable to it, and a wrong answer carries no trace of the process that produced it. [uncertain] whether any 2025-2026 item types capture intermediate work.
ai_tutor_diagnosis_reliability: There is no AI error-type diagnosis in IXL to validate, so the question of ground-truth validation does not arise - the honest finding is absence, not unreliability. What IS validated is the platform's overall achievement effect (ESSA Tier 1 and Tier 2 studies, below) and, indirectly, the adaptive engine. Known failure modes relevant to us: (1) the answer-only channel means the 'correct answer trap' is structural - a lucky guess raises SmartScore identically to genuine understanding; (2) SmartScore is widely criticised by students and parents as punitive, since a wrong answer near the top of a skill drops the score sharply and can wipe out substantial progress, which drives frustration, guessing and answer-seeking behaviour (an entire cottage industry of third-party IXL answer solvers and AI helpers exists precisely because of this dynamic) - and guessing further corrupts whatever diagnostic signal the answer stream carries; (3) Trouble Spots' three-miss trigger is a threshold heuristic with no published validation that three misses indicates a real, stable, remediable difficulty rather than fatigue or inattention.
evidence_quote: On Trouble Spots, from IXL's own teacher-facing material: 'IXL identifies a trouble spot when a student has missed three questions within a specific item type in a skill', and the report 'shows you which learners are having problems with that particular item type as well as missed questions you can scroll through.' On the Diagnostic, from IXL's official FAQ: 'A student's diagnostic level represents their working grade level. So a level of 400 represents a readiness to start working on 4th grade skills' - and the same FAQ makes no mention whatsoever of misconceptions or error types. On what parents get: 'IXL automatically creates a personalized learning plan of the exact skills your child is ready to learn next.' Note the noun in every case: skills and levels, never kinds of mistakes.
how_parent_involved: gatekeeper + dashboard-only, and in the dominant school-assigned use case closer to passive. Family memberships make the parent the account holder and payer (gatekeeper), with a parent icon and a Reports tab giving progress, usage time, SmartScores, trouble spots and diagnostic levels. But IXL's centre of gravity is the classroom: most children encounter IXL because a teacher assigns it, and the parent then sees a score dashboard for work they did not set. Either way the parent receives numbers - SmartScore 62, diagnostic level 430, three trouble spots - and no narrative of what went wrong or any script for what to say. IXL even publishes a 'How can I get parents involved?' guide for teachers, which itself signals that default parent involvement is thin.
ai_tutor_directly_to_child: no. IXL has no conversational AI tutor that talks to a child. When a child answers incorrectly, IXL shows a static, pre-authored step-by-step walkthrough of the correct solution for that problem, and 'Learn with an example' shows a worked example of the skill - both are canonical explanations of how the problem SHOULD be solved, generated from the item, not a response to what this particular child actually did. Live Message inside Live Classroom is a teacher typing to a student, not AI. IXL's AI investment is teacher-facing (Spark Studio for content creation), and its human tutoring lives in the separately acquired MyTutor. The strongest indirect evidence of this gap is the third-party ecosystem - tools like Pengi explicitly market themselves as 'AI tutor for IXL' to fill the missing conversational layer.
key_finding: Verified: IXL's 'diagnostic' is difficulty re-calibration, not error-type classification. The Real-Time Diagnostic answers 'what grade level is this child working at, per strand?' in about 45 minutes per subject, kept current by 10-15 questions a week; Trouble Spots answers 'which item type has this child missed three or more times?'. Neither answers 'is this a reading error, a conceptual misconception, or a calculation slip?' - and IXL's own documentation never uses that vocabulary. The structural cause is the input channel: IXL only observes final answers (MCQ, typed values, drag-and-drop), so the child's reasoning process is never captured and therefore cannot be classified. This is the market gap in its clearest form. IXL is the most sophisticated, best-evidenced adaptive practice platform in the world for primary math (ESSA Tier 1 RCT), it has been at this for two decades, it has the largest response dataset in the category, and it still stops at 'which skill' rather than 'which kind of mistake' - and it still hands the parent a number rather than an explanation. Add the Indonesian-market barriers (English-only, roughly IDR 150,000-320,000/month, no Kurikulum Merdeka alignment, no offline design, no AI tutor speaking to the child) and IXL is not a defensible incumbent in this segment on either the diagnosis axis or the parent axis.
study_scale_or_sample: Multiple independent efficacy evaluations, but all of the whole platform rather than of any diagnostic mechanism. (1) A randomized controlled trial conducted by Johns Hopkins University in which IXL Math students outperformed control by an average of 10 points on the Star Math assessment, meeting ESSA Tier 1 and What Works Clearinghouse standards; gains were larger for Hispanic, Special Education, English Language Learner and FARMS subgroups, in the range of 13-17 points. (2) An SRI International-reviewed three-year quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control-group study across grades 3-8, finding statistically significant larger gains in IXL schools than in comparable non-IXL schools, meeting ESSA Tier 2 (moderate evidence) and WWC standards with reservations (ERIC ED628125). [uncertain] exact student sample sizes and school counts for both studies - the press releases and summaries do not consistently state n.
evidence_strength: strong for the negative finding, strong-but-off-target for efficacy. The claim that IXL does not classify error types is well supported: it rests on IXL's own official teacher guides, its Diagnostic FAQ, its user guides and its product pages, in all of which the vocabulary is uniformly skills, levels and item types, with misconception and error type entirely absent - and it is corroborated by the mechanism (three-miss threshold; answer-only input). The efficacy evidence is genuinely strong by edtech standards (ESSA Tier 1 RCT plus Tier 2 quasi-experiment) but is vendor-commissioned and measures the whole product, so it cannot be read as evidence for the diagnostic layer specifically.
remediation_efficacy_evidence: Yes for the platform, no for the diagnosis mechanism - an important distinction for our gap thesis. IXL can point to the strongest evidence base in this competitor set: a Johns Hopkins RCT meeting ESSA Tier 1 and WWC standards (+10 points on Star Math, 13-17 points for several underserved subgroups) and an SRI-reviewed three-year quasi-experimental study meeting ESSA Tier 2. But every one of these tests the bundle - adaptive sequencing, spaced practice, volume of items, teacher assignment, step-by-step explanations - not the isolated contribution of identifying what kind of mistake a child makes. Since IXL never produces an error-type diagnosis, no study can show that such a diagnosis improves outcomes. The claim 'diagnosing error type improves learning' therefore remains empirically open in the commercial market, which is simultaneously the opportunity and the risk for a product built on that premise.
